disclosures.name: TestFreeOSMemory
disclosures.reason: the test allocates 32 MB inline in its own frame, clears the only named reference, and then asserts — from inside that same still-running frame — that FreeOSMemory has returned the memory to the OS. Go's per-safepoint liveness maps drop the allocation at its last use; the CLR reports a frame's slots live for the frame's whole lifetime, so the 32 MB is still rooted while the test is looking. Measured by the routing probe as a three-way control: the identical allocation behind a RETURNED call releases 33,689,600 B to the byte, and the inline form does not, invariant under Release and under untiered JIT. The first assert (HeapReleased must increase at all) PASSES on the S2/S3 high-water surface — 3,031,040 B of unrelated memory really is released — which is why the pin is the second assert's prefix and stops before its run-varying byte counts

disclosures.name: TestPanicOnFault
disclosures.reason: The first member of the host-fatal class (coordinator ruling, 2026-09-02), and the class exists because this test does not DIVERGE -- it takes the process down, so every test after it in its phase is lost too. panic_test.go mmaps a PROT_READ page and writes to it, expecting SetPanicOnFault(true) to convert the hardware fault into a recoverable panic. Go installs a SIGSEGV handler and recovers; the CLR on Linux has no SEH equivalent and the process dies. MEASURED cost: the host reports ONE verdict (TestFreeOSMemory, first alphabetically) and tests 2..10 are a contiguous alphabetical tail of absences with no results file written -- so the failure is worth NINE verdicts, not one, which is what makes an exclusion the right instrument rather than a per-test disclosure. Withdrawn from BOTH sides by name (go test -skip and the converted host's --skip, ONE string handed to each so the two runs filter identically) and COUNTED IN DISCLOSED -- never hidden: the row banks its matched count plus this entry, never a smaller total with the test quietly gone. That accounting is what distinguishes a bankable exclusion from the gated -test-filter census the doctrine forbids: this one is named in the committed manifest with a class and a reason, auditable in the same place as every other disclosure, and visible in the published counts. It passes the class's mint rule -- no committed proof page records it as a matching verdict -- and that is not luck of drafting but a checkable fact: panic_test.go carries //go:build aix || darwin || dragonfly || freebsd || linux || netbsd || openbsd, so the test does not exist on Windows at all and that proof page lists nine tests without it. The signature is deliberately EMPTY: a host-fatal test produces no verdict on either side to match a signature against, and matchTerminalStatuses refuses this class as a failure absorber precisely so a running-but-failing test can never be laundered through it. Self-retiring: the entry stops applying the moment the managed runtime can recover a hardware fault as a panic, with no corpus change and no manifest edit.

disclosures.name: TestWriteHeapDumpFinalizers
disclosures.signature: WriteHeapDump is not supported by the managed runtime
disclosures.reason: Go's heap-dump format is a serialization of the Go heap through Go's own type descriptors; the heap a managed build would describe is not a Go heap and has no such descriptors, so any managed rendering would be fabrication rather than implementation and no truthful form exists at any cost. Pinned AS FAILING under the class's binding anti-laundering clause: this test checks only that the dump is non-empty and never parses it, so a one-byte write would pass it while proving nothing — writing that byte is forbidden by this class's own text
